chapter_name: DSM-5 as a Framework for Psychiatric Diagnosis
chapter_title: DSM-5 as a Framework for Psychiatric Diagnosis

questions.question_text: Why is DSM-5 titled with an Arabic numeral rather than a Roman one?

options.text: This numbering convention was intended to symbolize the extent of the changes from DSM-IV and DSM-IV-TR.
This numbering convention was part of a general effort to make medical terminology less obscure.
This numbering convention followed the switch from Roman numerals to Arabic ones in the 2001 International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD).
This numbering convention was felt to be more conducive to labeling updates likely to fall between DSM-5 and DSM-6.
DSM-V was already trademarked.

correct_answer.text: This numbering convention was felt to be more conducive to labeling updates likely to fall between DSM-5 and DSM-6.

correct_answers.text: This numbering convention was felt to be more conducive to labeling updates likely to fall between DSM-5 and DSM-6.

questions.explanation: The new version of DSM was christened with an Arabic numeral, and updates will be numbered as with updated versions of computer software (DSM-5.1, DSM-5.2, etc.). This change in publishing and ease in communicating suggest that revisions can be undertaken in a series of smaller and timelier updates by a “permanent revision infrastructure,” and only when needed for specific disorders. This change may also spare future major revisions from needing such a large mobilization of experts to rewrite the system two decades after DSM-5 is first published (Regier et al. 2009). Initial revisions of DSM-5 are likely to result from the introduction of new technology, such as clinical or biological measures similar to those recommended for assessing cognitive impairment and sleep disorders

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD) is true?

options.text: All member countries of the World Health Organization (WHO) have agreed to use the ICD, which is uniform across countries, to report disease statistics to the WHO's surveillance system.

Most member countries of WHO have agreed to use the ICD to report disease statistics to the WHO's surveillance system, but in the United States, American Psychiatric Association guidelines recommend the use of DSM-5.

All member countries of WHO have agreed to use the ICD to report disease statistics to the WHO's surveillance system, but each country that uses the ICD has the ability to make changes to it for local use.
DSM-5 eliminates the distinction between DSM and ICD by providing ICD numbers alongside DSM numbers.
Both DSM and ICD are used in the United States to report disease statistics.

correct_answer.text: All member countries of WHO have agreed to use the ICD to report disease statistics to the WHO's surveillance system, but each country that uses the ICD has the ability to make changes to it for local use.

correct_answers.text: All member countries of WHO have agreed to use the ICD to report disease statistics to the WHO's surveillance system, but each country that uses the ICD has the ability to make changes to it for local use.

questions.explanation: Whereas the current classification for psychiatric practice in the United States is the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association 2013), the “official” classification for public health reporting is the ICD, developed and periodically revised by the World Health Organization. All member countries of WHO have agreed to use this system to report disease statistics to its surveillance system, although they may not adopt each updated version as soon as it is available. Each country does have the ability to make its own changes, for example, to include terms that are used locally or to add precision to the system. In the United States, the National Center for Health Statistics oversees this process, which produces a “clinical modification” of ICD. It collaborates with specialty organizations, such as the American Psychiatric Association, to incorporate diagnostic categories used in the United States.

questions.question_text: How does DSM-5 differ from DSM-IV in its conceptualization of mental disorders?

options.text: Whereas DSM-IV stated that mental disorders are usually associated with significant distress or impairment of performance, DSM-5 requires distress, disability, and/or increased risk of death, pain, disability, or loss of freedom to be present to diagnose a mental disorder.
Whereas DSM-IV did not address underlying causes, DSM-5 includes underlying causes as part of its definition of a mental disorder.
Whereas DSM-IV did not provide operational guidance on specifying a threshold for diagnosis, DSM-5 does provide such guidance.
Whereas DSM-IV provided operational guidance on specifying a threshold for diagnosis, DSM-5 does not.
Whereas DSM-IV disorders required 'significant distress or impairment' to establish the diagnosis, DSM-5 disorders do not.

correct_answer.text: Whereas DSM-IV did not address underlying causes, DSM-5 includes underlying causes as part of its definition of a mental disorder.

correct_answers.text: Whereas DSM-IV did not address underlying causes, DSM-5 includes underlying causes as part of its definition of a mental disorder.

questions.explanation: When there is no way to identify the causal factors or mechanisms of an illness, and the clinical presentation does not produce a clear break between normality and clinically relevant illness, specifying when a syndrome crosses the boundary from normal to abnormal is one of the challenges for a classification system (Kendell and Jablensky 2003). In DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association 1994), this challenge was met by requiring the association of a syndrome with distress, impairment, or risk of other harmful outcomes. More than 70% of the specific disorders in DSM-IV included distress or impairment among the required criteria for the condition. In DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013), the definition of mental disorder is phrased in terms of dysfunctions and their underlying processes: “A mental disorder is a syndrome characterized by clinically significant disturbance in an individual’s cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior that reflects a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning. Mental disorders are usually associated with significant distress or disability in social, occupational, or other important activities” (p. 20). This definition still does not provide operational guidance on specifying a threshold for diagnosis. The difficulty in determining when a dysfunction has produced a change from normal variation to pathology has meant that the coupling to “significant distress or impairment” could not be removed completely. DSM-5 criteria for some individual disorders have retained DSM-IV’s specific reliance on distress or impairment to establish the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: What were the two categories of mental disorders in the United States Census from 1840 through 1890?

options.text: Psychosis and neurosis.
Schizophrenia and neurosis.
Insanity and idiocy.
Insanity and neurosis.
Idiocy and neurosis.

questions.explanation: From 1840 through 1890, the U.S. Census attempted to count people who had a mental disorder, characterized as “insanity” or “idiocy.” In 1880, a special Census survey tried to apply a system with seven categories, but officials found it impossible to construct a list that would be endorsed by leadersof psychiatry and psychology (American Psychiatric Association 1952). After 1890, the Census abandoned its effort to determine psychiatric illness in the population

questions.question_text: What was the major distinction between psychiatric illnesses in DSM-I?

options.text: Organic versus nonorganic.
Neurotic versus psychotic.
Psychiatric versus neurological.
Childhood onset versus adult onset.
Treatable versus untreatable.

questions.explanation: The logic of the classification used in DSM-I (American Psychiatric Association 1952) applied the major viewpoints in American psychiatry at the time (Grob 1991). Illnesses were classified as either organic or nonorganic; within the nonorganic category, psychoneurotic disorders were defined in psychodynamic terms, and within psychoneurotic disorders, specific “reactions” were defined in Adolf Meyer’s life-history terms.

questions.question_text: Which DSM edition was the first to provide explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, offer extensive information beyond the criteria sets to help clinicians understand the described disorders, and eliminate the term 'neurosis'?

options.text: DSM-III (1980).
DSM-III-Revised (1987).
DSM-IV-Revised (2000).

questions.explanation: In 1974, Robert Spitzer, one of the leaders in these efforts to improve reliability, became chair of the American Psychiatric Association Task Force on Nomenclature and Statistics to prepare DSM-III (American Psychiatric Association 1980). He recruited task force members largely from the growing clinical research community, and their commitment to enhance clinical and research diagnoses led to a new paradigm for classifying mental disorders (Klerman et al. 1984). DSM-III provided an explicit set of criteria for each clinical disorder. These criteria specified characteristics that must be present insome combination (“inclusion criteria”) and characteristics that would prevent the disorder from being diagnosed (“exclusion criteria”). DSM-III dropped the concept of psychoneurotic disorders that had been introduced in the army’s nomenclature and also removed the term neurosis from the classification system. Rather than giving a brief one- or two-sentence definition of a disorder, DSM-III provided extensive information beyond the criteria sets in an effort to help clinicians understand the disorder; typically, each disorder also contained a description of associated features, course of illness, and differential diagnosis (Spitzer et al. 1980)

questions.question_text: Which DSM edition was the first to formally place an emphasis on clinical utility, require that changes from a previous DSM edition be based on empirical research, and establish eligibility criteria to minimize the influence of commercial and other interests in selection of disorders or formulation of criteria?

options.text: DSM-III (1980).
DSM-III Revised (1987).
DSM-IV Text Revision (2000).

questions.explanation: As for DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association 1994), guidelines established at the initial stages of planning for DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013) included an emphasis on clinical relevance. This emphasis was coupled with a requirement that significant changes from DSMIV should be based on empirical research. To address the growing worry that commercial and other interests might hope to influence the selection of disorders or the formulation of their criteria, the American Psychiatric Association Board of Trustees developed eligibility criteria to ensure the independence of participants in any level of the revision work.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a change made in DSM-5?

options.text: Asperger's syndrome and autistic disorder were combined.
Substance abuse and substance dependence were combined.
Panic disorder and agoraphobia were unlinked.
Bulimia nervosa and anorexia nervosa were unlinked.
Several of the somatoform disorders were grouped into a single category of somatic symptom disorder.

correct_answer.text: Bulimia nervosa and anorexia nervosa were unlinked.

correct_answers.text: Bulimia nervosa and anorexia nervosa were unlinked.

questions.explanation: Bulimia and anorexia are still included as eating disorders, although some of the criteria have been changed. In DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013), five disorders previously distinguished as separate categories were combined into a single autism spectrum disorder. For substance use disorders, the categories of abuse and dependence were collapsed, and a dimensional approach was used to grade the severity of dependence. Agoraphobia and panic disorder were simplified by uncoupling the disorders and presenting two separate disorders defined without regard to the presence or absence of the other. Several of the DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association 1994) somatoform disorders are now grouped into a single category, somatic symptom disorder, based on common features of somatic symptoms and cognitive distortions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a change made in the revision from DSM-IV-TR to DSM-5?

options.text: Binge-eating disorder was removed as a diagnosis.
A bereavement exclusion was added to the criteria for major depressive disorder.
Bizarre delusions and Schneiderian first-rank hallucinations were given greater prominence in the diagnosis of schizophrenia.
Minor neurocognitive disorder was added as a diagnosis.
Gambling disorder was moved to Impulse Disorders Not Elsewhere Classified.

correct_answer.text: Minor neurocognitive disorder was added as a diagnosis.

correct_answers.text: Minor neurocognitive disorder was added as a diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Minor neurocognitive disorder has been added to DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013), because clinical and epidemiological data have demonstrated the presence of a clinical condition that does not reach the severity of major neurocognitive disorder but nevertheless requires assessment, care, and follow-up. Revisions to the criteria for schizophrenia included removal of the special significance given to bizarre delusions and Schneiderian first-rank hallucinations in DSM-IV-TR (American Psychiatric Association 2000) and deletion of the five subtypes of schizophrenia. The bereavement exclusion was eliminated from the criteria for major depressive disorder, although language was included to clarify that grief reactions are not automatically considered evidence of a major depressive disorder. In DSM-5, binge-eating disorder was added as a diagnosis in a new “Feeding and Eating Disorders” chapter, and gambling disorder was moved from the DSM-IV-TR chapter “Impulse Disorders Not Elsewhere Classified” to the “Substance Use and Other Addictive Disorders” chapter

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly identifies the reason that the DSM-5 Work Group chose not to revise the personality disorders classification by adopting a hybrid system combining the traditional categorical model and a new model using quantitative ratings of personality domains and traits?

options.text: There was too much resistance from psychiatrists to giving up the current system.
The work group decided that more study was required.
The work group rejected this change on the basis that such a system would unnecessarily retain the prejudices of the multiaxial system.
The work group rejected this change on the grounds that dimensional measurements would introduce too much subjectivity.
The work group rejected this change on the basis that retaining any of the previous system was likely to preserve the poor reliability of that system.

correct_answer.text: The work group decided that more study was required.

correct_answers.text: The work group decided that more study was required.

questions.explanation: In the approach considered, four of the prior personality disorder types would have been eliminated from the classification. To assess the patient, a clinician would determine if there was impairment in either 1) self-identity/ self-direction or 2) interpersonal functioning, as in intimacy and empathy. If so, and if one of the six remaining types is present, a diagnosis for that specific disorder would be given. This approach intrigued the task force, but the peer review committees felt it was not well enough established to be incorporated into the manual for routine clinical use. Section III of DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013) contains this alternative model for personality disorders, which will need more study before being formally incorporated into the classification system at some future date.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements correctly identifies how DSM-5 cross-cutting measures and dimensional diagnoses differ in their intended use?

options.text: Dimensional diagnoses are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits, whereas cross-cutting measures are used when a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked.
Cross-cutting measures are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits, whereas dimensional diagnoses are used when a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked.
Both dimensional diagnoses and cross-cutting measures are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits.
Both dimensional diagnoses and cross-cutting measures are meant to be used whenever a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked.
A cross-cutting measure is one special case of a dimensional diagnosis.

correct_answer.text: Cross-cutting measures are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits, whereas dimensional diagnoses are used when a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked.

correct_answers.text: Cross-cutting measures are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits, whereas dimensional diagnoses are used when a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked.

questions.explanation: A dimensional diagnosis is one special case of a dimensional measure. In DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2013), the cross-cutting measures are dimensional but are not specific to any disorder, as a dimensional diagnosis would be. Cross-cutting measures are meant to be used at periodic clinic visits, whereas dimensional diagnoses are used when a specific diagnosis needs to be established or checked. Cross-cutting measures are meant for longitudinal follow-up of patients, particularly for management purposes, whereas dimensional diagnoses determine clinical status at one time point to guide decision making in the next time span. Cross-cutting measures may sometimes remind clinicians to check certain diagnoses, but are generally not screening measures themselves.

questions.question_text: The DSM-5 autism spectrum disorder and somatic symptom disorder categories were created to address which of the following issues?

options.text: Extensive comorbidity of diagnoses.
Increasing demands to use cross-cutting measures.
Pressure from the pharmaceutical industry.
Poor reliability and conceptual overlap between diagnoses.
Poor validity of diagnoses.

correct_answer.text: Poor reliability and conceptual overlap between diagnoses.

correct_answers.text: Poor reliability and conceptual overlap between diagnoses.

questions.explanation: From the beginning of the DSM-5 process, the extensive rate of co-occurrence of mental disorders had been identified as a concern. Research has not yet clarified the possible explanations of this apparent comorbidity: Does it reflect varying presentations of a single, underlying condition that has been fragmented into separate disorders; or a shared pathway of different conditions; or the production of one disorder by a preexisting one? One approach to the issue was to consider whether different groupings of disorders—that is, lumping rather than splitting—would offer a new, more useful way to account for these presentations. The proposal for a new “metastructure” was not adopted, because the empirical basis is underdeveloped for such a rethinking. The DSM-IV categoriesthat were collapsed into a broader-spectrum disorder were closely related and thought to represent unnecessary distinctions among a closely related set of conditions. The creation of these new, broader categories (autism spectrum disorder and somatic symptom disorder) was not aimed at addressing comorbidity so much as poor reliability and conceptual overlap. Development of a new metastructure to use in classifying disorders awaits more definitive research that accounts for the comorbidity.
